crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Forecasting research trends sits in citation mapping and discovery, part of The AI Researcher. It covers citation graphs, co-authorship, keyword and claim extraction, and temporal signals from publication and citation counts. It also touches adjacent entities such as models, tools, and glossary terms when they are linked to papers. The site catalogues 798 scientific models, 732 AI tools, and 686 glossary terms, and those entities can be linked to papers as trend signals. The aim is not to predict a single winner but to map shifting attention across a field.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on citation indexes, paper metadata, full texts, and extracted claims, plus compute for graph analysis and model training. A typical stack includes a bibliographic database, a graph store, a text pipeline, and a dashboard or API for exploration. The site's own library, currently 135 research papers with 12993 claims extracted from research works, is one small corpus of this kind. It can also draw on catalogued models, tools, and glossary terms when those are linked to the literature.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A common method starts with a citation graph and adds text signals from titles, abstracts, and extracted claims. Analysts compute co-citation, bibliographic coupling, centrality, and burst scores, then fit temporal models to rank emerging topics. Claim extraction can add finer-grained evidence about what papers assert, beyond what citation counts alone show. Validation often compares forecasts against later citations or expert review, and results are reported with uncertainty.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this area turn on the provenance of citation data, the license terms of full texts, and the accuracy of extracted claims. Citation counts can reflect age, venue prestige, and self-citation rather than quality, so trend forecasts can amplify existing biases. A sound practice is to record the source, version, and extraction date for every signal and to link to the original paper rather than a search tool. This site follows that rule by linking to original papers and not to the Consensus search tool. Privacy and author attribution also matter when co-authorship or reviewer data is used.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward richer temporal models, embedding-based citation prediction, and real-time monitoring of preprints and conference proceedings. Open citation infrastructure and better claim extraction are likely to make forecasts more granular and more reproducible. Expect more work on explainable trend signals, so a forecast can be traced back to specific papers, claims, or graph patterns. The main open question is how to separate durable shifts in a field from short-lived bursts of attention.
